title: Only a messenger
hook: Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers passed before him (3:144)

segments.voice: Yesterday: nudawiluha, the days take turns after Uhud, and your line, days turn.

In the chaos at Uhud, someone shouted that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had been killed. He hadn't; he was wounded, and his companions closed around him. But the rumor ran through the army faster than the truth. Some men put down their swords and sat. Some started thinking about running. If he was gone, what was left? The commentators say a verse came down about that moment. And years later, on the day he really did die, someone stood up and read it aloud.
screen: `A RUMOR AT UHUD.` → `IF HE WAS GONE, WHAT WAS LEFT?` → `READ ALOUD YEARS LATER.`

segments.voice: The verse is 3:144. In Pickthall's words: "Muhammad is but a messenger, messengers (the like of whom) have passed away before him." Then it asks: if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels? Whoever turns back doesn't harm God at all. A startling verse to find in scripture: a plain statement that the Prophet is mortal, and that faith isn't meant to hang on one human life. Now the second scene. Medina, years later. The Prophet has died in the room of his wife A'ishah. Umar, a companion known for his strength, can't accept it; he stands in the mosque insisting it isn't true. Then Abu Bakr arrives, the Prophet's close friend and companion. He goes in, uncovers the Prophet's face, and kisses him. Then he comes out to the crowd. According to the account in Sahih al-Bukhari, he says: whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; and whoever worships God, God is alive and does not die. And he recites 3:144. The report says it was as if people had never heard the verse before, and then everyone was reciting it. Umar said his legs gave way when he heard it. A hadith in Bukhari ties faith to loving the Prophet more than one's own parent and child. And still the Qur'an itself says he was a man, a messenger, one in a long line. What he brought, the prayer, the Qur'an, the way of living, is meant to keep going after him.
screen: `A RUMOR IN THE BATTLE` · `MUHAMMAD IS BUT A MESSENGER` · `ABU BAKR AT THE DOOR` · `GOD IS ALIVE AND DOES NOT DIE` · then, large: `THE MESSAGE OUTLIVES THE MESSENGER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who taught you something that mattered and is no longer in your life: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend who moved away, someone who died. Instead of dwelling on the loss, ask what of theirs is still alive in you, a habit, a phrase, a way of treating people, and name it. If you pray, you can ask mercy for them.
Abu Bakr. The companion who, on the day the Prophet died, recited 3:144 and said: whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died.
Your line: the message outlives the messenger. God is alive and does not die, Abu Bakr told the crowd. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims honor the Prophet as the final messenger while holding that he was a mortal man; 3:144 and Abu Bakr's words at his death are often recalled when teaching that faith rests on God, not on any person.

original.note: Arabic: and Muhammad is only a messenger (3:144).

trapdoor: what you thought: a prophet's followers would fall apart without him.
what it means: the Qur'an says plainly he is a mortal messenger, and faith is meant to outlive him.
what a scholar hears: a verse revealed for a false rumor at Uhud, then recited by Abu Bakr at the real death, as Bukhari reports.
recall: the good that is known, recognized

chat.says: When the Prophet died, how did his followers keep going?
options: Abu Bakr recited 3:144: Muhammad is a messenger; God is alive and doesn't die.
They decided the message ended with him, and most went back home.
They stopped praying until a new prophet came along to lead them.
chat.meaning: Sahih al-Bukhari: whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; whoever worships God, God is alive and does not die. Then he recited 3:144.
